blocks.html: Latency
Definition: Delay between request initiation and completion of response.
blocks.text: Definition: Delay between request initiation and completion of response.

blocks.html: Types of Latency:
Network latency: Time taken for a packet to travel from source to destination.
blocks.text: Network latency: Time taken for a packet to travel from source to destination.

blocks.html: Disk latency: Time taken to read/write data on storage.
blocks.text: Disk latency: Time taken to read/write data on storage.

blocks.html: Memory latency: Time between issuing a memory request and receiving the data.
blocks.text: Memory latency: Time between issuing a memory request and receiving the data.

blocks.html: CPU latency: Time to execute an instruction.
blocks.text: CPU latency: Time to execute an instruction.

blocks.html: Components:
Propagation delay (signal travel time).
Transmission delay (pushing data onto medium).
Queuing delay (waiting in buffer/queue).
Processing delay (time to process the request).
blocks.text: Processing delay (time to process the request).

blocks.html: Measurement: Latency is measured as time duration (ns, µs, ms) depending on context.
blocks.text: Measurement: Latency is measured as time duration (ns, µs, ms) depending on context.

blocks.html: Throughput
Definition: Rate of successful data transfer or operations per second.
blocks.text: Definition: Rate of successful data transfer or operations per second.

blocks.html: Formula:
Determinants:
Resource availability (Bandwidth, CPU, memory, disk).
How much work is competing (if too many tasks fight for resources, throughput drops).
blocks.text: How much work is competing (if too many tasks fight for resources, throughput drops).

blocks.html: Overheads (extra work like protocol headers or waiting in queues).
blocks.text: Overheads (extra work like protocol headers or waiting in queues).

blocks.html: Measurement: Transactions/sec, Mbps, IOPS (Input/Output operations per second).
blocks.text: Measurement: Transactions/sec, Mbps, IOPS (Input/Output operations per second).

blocks.html: Performance Limits
Little’s Law:
What Little’s Law really requires
The system must be stable (the rate at which requests arrive ≈ the rate at which requests depart).
blocks.text: The system must be stable (the rate at which requests arrive ≈ the rate at which requests depart).

blocks.html: Requests enter, get processed, and leave — without queues growing infinitely.
blocks.text: Requests enter, get processed, and leave — without queues growing infinitely.

blocks.html: Example:
Setup: Server has 2 worker threads.
Initially:
Latency = 0.5 s per request
Throughput = 4 req/s
Concurrency = 4 × 0.5 = 2 requests
After optimisations:
Latency = 0.25 s per request (after optimization)
Throughput = 8 req/s:
Concurrency = 8 × 0.25 = 2 requests
System Overload (Failure of Little’s law):
Requests come at rate 10 res/s.
Server can only process 4 req/s.
The extra 6 req/s pile up in the queue.
blocks.text: The extra 6 req/s pile up in the queue.

blocks.html: Latency grows continuously (queue wait + processing).
Throughput remains capped at 4 req/s.
Why Little’s Law fails here:
System is not stable (arrival rate > service rate).
blocks.text: System is not stable (arrival rate > service rate).

blocks.html:
Concurrency keeps increasing without bound, so
Concurrency = Throughput × Latency
no longer matches reality.
blocks.text: Concurrency keeps increasing without bound, so Concurrency = Throughput × Latency no longer matches reality.

blocks.html: Optimisation Techniques
Throughput
In practice, when you want to increase throughput, you often look at ways to use bandwidth more efficiently.

blocks.html: Bandwidth ≠ Throughput:
Bandwidth = maximum capacity for the data transfer of the link.
blocks.text: Bandwidth = maximum capacity for the data transfer of the link.

blocks.html: Throughput = actual data transfer achieved, so it cannot exceed bandwidth.
blocks.text: Throughput = actual data transfer achieved, so it cannot exceed bandwidth.

blocks.html: Reduce the wasted bandwidth
Offloading load - Shifting/distributing work away from the main/origin server (or bottleneck resource)
blocks.text: Offloading load - Shifting/distributing work away from the main/origin server (or bottleneck resource)

blocks.html: Bandwidth
Data Compression
Compress files, images, or responses before transmission.
blocks.text: Compress files, images, or responses before transmission.

blocks.html: Effect: Fewer bytes sent → higher effective bandwidth.
blocks.text: Effect: Fewer bytes sent → higher effective bandwidth.

blocks.html: Content Delivery Network (CDN)
Place content closer to users via distributed edge servers.
blocks.text: Place content closer to users via distributed edge servers.

blocks.html: Effect: Offloads origin, reduces congestion, increases throughput,
blocks.text: Effect: Offloads origin, reduces congestion, increases throughput,

blocks.html: Multiplexing and Persistent Connections
Use HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 to send multiple requests over a single TCP/QUIC connection.
blocks.text: Use HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 to send multiple requests over a single TCP/QUIC connection.

blocks.html: TCP: Transmission Control Protocol
QUIC: Quick UDP Internet Connections
Effect: Reduces overhead of opening/closing multiple connections, improves utilization.
blocks.text: Effect: Reduces overhead of opening/closing multiple connections, improves utilization.

blocks.html: Caching
Browser caching, proxy caching, or edge caching.
blocks.text: Browser caching, proxy caching, or edge caching.

blocks.html: Effect: Reduces repeated transfers, increases available bandwidth for unique traffic.
blocks.text: Effect: Reduces repeated transfers, increases available bandwidth for unique traffic.

blocks.html: Load Balancing
Distribute requests across multiple servers.
Effect: Prevents one server from becoming a bottleneck, increases overall throughput.
blocks.text: Effect: Prevents one server from becoming a bottleneck, increases overall throughput.

blocks.html: Efficient Protocols
Choosing the best protocol as per the requirements can make data smaller (reduced header size or reduced size of data based on format), fewer retransmissions etc.
blocks.text: Choosing the best protocol as per the requirements can make data smaller (reduced header size or reduced size of data based on format), fewer retransmissions etc.

blocks.html: Latency
Reduce Network Hops
Fewer routers/switches in the request path.
blocks.text: Fewer routers/switches in the request path.

blocks.html: Use edge servers or regional data centers.
blocks.text: Use edge servers or regional data centers.

blocks.html: Effect: Shorter path → lower round-trip time (RTT).
blocks.text: Effect: Shorter path → lower round-trip time (RTT).

blocks.html: DNS Optimisation
Use faster DNS resolvers, DNS caching, or Anycast DNS.
blocks.text: Use faster DNS resolvers, DNS caching, or Anycast DNS.

blocks.html: Effect: Faster domain resolution reduces initial connection delay.
blocks.text: Effect: Faster domain resolution reduces initial connection delay.

blocks.html: Connection Reuse and Keep-Alive
Avoid re-establishing TCP/TLS handshakes for every request.
blocks.text: Avoid re-establishing TCP/TLS handshakes for every request.

blocks.html: Effect: Reduces handshake latency.
Asynchronous and Parallel Requests
Send independent requests in parallel rather than serial.
blocks.text: Send independent requests in parallel rather than serial.

blocks.html: Edge Computing
Process data closer to the user instead of central servers.
blocks.text: Process data closer to the user instead of central servers.

blocks.html: Effect: Cuts propagation delay.
Database Query Optimization
Use indexing, denormalization, caching, and query tuning.
blocks.text: Use indexing, denormalization, caching, and query tuning.

blocks.html: Effect: Reduces application-layer latency.
TCP/QUIC Optimizations
Enable TCP Fast Open, use QUIC (UDP-based, faster recovery from packet loss).
blocks.text: Enable TCP Fast Open, use QUIC (UDP-based, faster recovery from packet loss).

blocks.html: Effect: Faster connections, lower transport latency.
blocks.text: Effect: Faster connections, lower transport latency.

blocks.html: Reduce Payload Size
Minify JavaScript, CSS, bundle requests, use pagination in APIs.
blocks.text: Minify JavaScript, CSS, bundle requests, use pagination in APIs.

blocks.html: Effect: Less data per request → faster response.
blocks.text: Effect: Less data per request → faster response.

blocks.html: Common Misconceptions
Latency ≠ Response time (response time includes latency + processing overhead).
blocks.text: Latency ≠ Response time (response time includes latency + processing overhead).

blocks.html: High bandwidth ≠ Low latency. Bandwidth affects throughput, not latency.
blocks.text: High bandwidth ≠ Low latency. Bandwidth affects throughput, not latency.

blocks.html: Increasing throughput does not guarantee lower latency; may even worsen it if queues build up.
